title: Confidence-Bounded Unit-Test Rewards for Reinforcement Learning from Verifiable Rewards

raw.stage1:
### Purpose
The contribution's purpose is to address the noisy pass-rate reward in RLVR for code generation when only a small number \( m \) of unit tests can be executed per rollout. This specific problem of noisy rewards in RLVR for code generation is not directly addressed in any prior paper. While [4] discusses noisy rewards in RL generally, it does not focus on RLVR or the specific issue of limited unit tests in code generation. Similarly, [10] and [12] discuss challenges in RLVR but do not explicitly address the problem of noisy pass-rate rewards due to limited unit tests. Therefore, no prior paper covers this purpose.

### Mechanism
The mechanism involves using a Lower Confidence Bound (LCB) reward that models test outcomes as Bernoulli trials with a Beta prior and uses the delta-quantile of the Beta posterior as a conservative reward. This mechanism is a specific adaptation of confidence-bound-based methods to the RLVR setting. Papers such as [3], [9], and [20] discuss UCB-based methods and confidence bounds in bandit problems, including Bernoulli rewards, but they do not apply these methods to RLVR or code generation. [14] and [30] discuss pessimism in RL, but their approaches are not equivalent to the specific use of the Beta posterior's delta-quantile as a reward. Thus, the mechanism is not covered.

### Evaluation
The evaluation uses GRPO training and evaluates on MBPP+ and HumanEval+ against pass-rate and other reward baselines. The evaluation design — training with GRPO and comparing against reward baselines on standard RLVR benchmarks — is covered by [10], which also uses GRPO and evaluates on RLVR benchmarks like HumanEval. While the specific benchmarks (MBPP+ and HumanEval+) may differ, the evaluation design is not novel.

### Domain
The domain is RL for code generation, specifically RLVR. This domain is explicitly covered by [10], [12], and [19], which all focus on RLVR for code generation tasks. While the specific sub-problem (noisy pass-rate rewards with limited unit tests) may differ, the general application area of RLVR for code generation is not new.

**PURPOSE: Addresses noisy pass-rate reward in RLVR for code generation when only a small number m of unit tests can be executed per rollout.**

The purpose is specifically about handling reward noise/uncertainty arising from limited test execution in RLVR for code generation. Paper [4] addresses "noisy RL problems with perturbed rewards" but focuses on adversarial/sensor noise in general RL, not the specific problem of limited unit test sampling causing stochastic pass-rate estimates. Paper [8] addresses "reinforcement learning under limited feedback" where only a fraction of samples get rewards labeled — this is about which samples to label, not about noisy estimates from few tests. Paper [5] addresses RL for code generation but focuses on reasoning-process rewards, not noisy pass-rate estimation. Paper [11] addresses sparse rewards in CI testing (low failure rates), which is a different problem (sparsity vs. noise from limited test count). No prior paper specifically targets the problem of noisy pass-rate rewards due to limited unit test execution in RLVR. This purpose appears uncovered.

**MECHANISM: LCB reward using Beta posterior over Bernoulli trials, taking delta-quantile as conservative reward penalizing high-uncertainty solutions.**

This is a Bayesian lower confidence bound: model test outcomes as Bernoulli, place Beta prior, compute posterior, use a low quantile (conservative estimate) as reward. Paper [3] (KL-UCB) uses Bernoulli rewards with confidence bounds but for bandit exploration (upper bound, not lower). Paper [7] (Thompson Sampling / posterior sampling) uses Beta-Bernoulli posterior sampling for bandits. Paper [1] uses bootstrapping for Bernoulli bandits. Paper [9] (lil' UCB) uses UCB for bandit arm identification. Paper [6] uses uncertainty-penalized rewards in RLHF with ensemble-based uncertainty, penalizing high-uncertainty solutions — this is conceptually similar (conservative reward under uncertainty) but uses ensemble diversity rather than Beta-Bernoulli posterior quantile. Paper [23] uses pessimistic MLE in RLHF. Paper [27] (CQL) uses conservative Q-learning with pessimism. The specific primitive — Beta posterior over Bernoulli test outcomes, using a low quantile as reward — is closest to Beta-Bernoulli Thompson Sampling (paper [7]) but inverted (lower quantile instead of sample). Paper [6] penalizes uncertainty in rewards but via ensembles, not Beta-Bernoulli. The exact mechanism (Beta-Bernoulli posterior + lower quantile as reward signal in RLVR) does not appear in any prior paper. However, the underlying primitive of "use lower confidence bound from Beta-Bernoulli posterior" is essentially the Bayesian LCB for Bernoulli bandits, which is implicit in papers [3] and [7]. Paper [3] explicitly discusses Bernoulli rewards and KL-based confidence bounds. The Beta-Bernoulli LCB as a reward shaping mechanism in RL training is not directly present. I'll mark this NONE as no paper uses this exact primitive as a reward signal in RL training.

GRPO is used in paper [12] ("RLVR training with GRPO improves MATH-500 performance"). HumanEval and MBPP are standard code generation benchmarks used in papers [5] and [10]. The evaluation design — using GRPO as the RL algorithm and evaluating on HumanEval+/MBPP+ — uses the same benchmark family (HumanEval, MBPP) and same RL framework (GRPO) as papers [5] and [12]. Paper [5] explicitly evaluates on HumanEval and MBPP with RL training. This evaluation design is covered.

**DOMAIN: RL for code generation (RLVR)**

Papers [5], [10], and [17] all work in RL for code generation. Paper [5] is explicitly "Reinforcing Code Generation." Paper [10] is "Training Software Engineering Agents via... Rewards."
